claims.source: Due to its ability to rapidly spread in contaminated water, cholera poses a serious world health risk, affecting between 1 and 4 million people and causing 21,000–143,000 deaths per year, especially in poor or underdeveloped countries (WHO, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO 2019 data.

claims.claim: V. cholerae acquire new phenotypes through horizontal gene transfer (HGT).
claims.source: One way in which V. cholerae acquire new phenotypes is through horizontal gene transfer (HGT), which is the direct movement of DNA from one organism to another.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial evolution mechanisms.

claims.claim: Natural competence for transformation allows bacteria to absorb free DNA from their surroundings using their competence-induced DNA-uptake complex.
claims.source: A major mode of HGT is natural competence for transformation in which bacteria are able to absorb free DNA from their surroundings using their competence-induced DNA-uptake complex (Chen and Dubnau, 2004; Johnston et al., 2014; Matthey and Blokesch, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: When sufficient homology is present between the incoming DNA and the bacterial genome, the absorbed genetic material can be integrated into the genome via double homologous recombination.
claims.source: When sufficient homology is present between the incoming DNA and the bacterial genome, the absorbed genetic material can be integrated into the genome via double homologous recombination at the expense of the initial DNA region.
claims.evidence: This describes the established mechanism of homologous recombination in transformation.

claims.claim: V. cholerae gained an ~40 kbp O139-antigen cluster at the expense of the original ~30 kbp O1-antigen cluster through natural transformation.
claims.source: As an example of the significant power of this natural competence for gene uptake, we previously witnessed the gain of an ~40 kbp O139-antigen cluster at the expense of the original ~30 kbp O1-antigen cluster through natural transformation (followed by strong selective pressure exerted by antibiotics or phages; Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2007), which significantly changed the phenotypes of these bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is a previous finding by the authors, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Griffith's experiment in 1928 unambiguously proved that transformation contributes to evolution and pathogen emergence.
claims.source: And while Griffith's experiment in 1928 unambiguously proved that transformation contributes to evolution and pathogen emergence, the general prevalence of non-degraded DNA with sufficient coding capacity has been questioned (Nielsen et al., 2007; Overballe-Petersen et al., 2013; Croucher et al., 2016), drawing inquiries as to whether this mode of HGT could be responsible for the major changes causing pandemic strains to emerge.
claims.evidence: This references the historical Griffith experiment and subsequent questioning in the literature.

claims.claim: The induction of competence in V. cholerae is tightly regulated.
claims.source: The induction of competence in V. cholerae is tightly regulated (recently reviewed by Metzger and Blokesch, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claims.claim: V. cholerae becomes naturally competent for genetic transformation upon growth on chitin-rich exoskeletons of zooplankton.
claims.source: Briefly, upon growth on the (molted) chitin-rich exoskeletons of zooplankton (Pruzzo et al., 2008), the most abundant polysaccharide in the aquatic environment and therefore an important carbon source for chitinolytic bacteria (Gooday, 1990), the expression pattern of V. cholerae is altered (Meibom et al., 2004) to render it naturally competent for genetic transformation (Meibom et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Chitin is the most abundant polysaccharide in the aquatic environment.
claims.source: Briefly, upon growth on the (molted) chitin-rich exoskeletons of zooplankton (Pruzzo et al., 2008), the most abundant polysaccharide in the aquatic environment and therefore an important carbon source for chitinolytic bacteria (Gooday, 1990), the expression pattern of V. cholerae is altered (Meibom et al., 2004) to render it naturally competent for genetic transformation (Meibom et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gooday, 1990.

claims.claim: When chitin degradation products are sensed by V. cholerae, it produces the regulatory protein TfoX.
claims.source: Initially, when chitin degradation products are sensed by V. cholerae, it produces the regulatory protein TfoX (Li and Roseman, 2004; Meibom et al., 2004; Meibom et al., 2005; Yamamoto et al., 2011; Dalia et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: TfoX positively regulates the expression of the major DNA-uptake machinery in V. cholerae.
claims.source: This competence activator positively regulates the expression of the major DNA-uptake machinery in the cell (Matthey and Blokesch, 2016), providing a direct connection between growth on chitin and competence activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: HapR acts as repressor of dns, which encodes an extracellular nuclease that inhibits transformation.
claims.source: Apart from TfoX, natural competence and transformation also depend on the master regulator of quorum sensing, HapR, in two ways: i) HapR acts as repressor of dns, which encodes an extracellular nuclease that inhibits transformation (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008); and ii) HapR together with TfoX co-activates the transcription factor QstR, which further represses dns as well as activates several DNA-uptake genes (Lo Scrudato and Blokesch, 2013; Jaskólska et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: HapR together with TfoX co-activates the transcription factor QstR.
claims.source: Apart from TfoX, natural competence and transformation also depend on the master regulator of quorum sensing, HapR, in two ways: i) HapR acts as repressor of dns, which encodes an extracellular nuclease that inhibits transformation (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008); and ii) HapR together with TfoX co-activates the transcription factor QstR, which further represses dns as well as activates several DNA-uptake genes (Lo Scrudato and Blokesch, 2013; Jaskólska et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: QstR represses dns and activates several DNA-uptake genes.
claims.source: Apart from TfoX, natural competence and transformation also depend on the master regulator of quorum sensing, HapR, in two ways: i) HapR acts as repressor of dns, which encodes an extracellular nuclease that inhibits transformation (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008); and ii) HapR together with TfoX co-activates the transcription factor QstR, which further represses dns as well as activates several DNA-uptake genes (Lo Scrudato and Blokesch, 2013; Jaskólska et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Environmental DNA is often heavily degraded and therefore short in size.
claims.source: While the chitin-induced DNA-uptake complex of V. cholerae is able to absorb DNA from the surrounding (Seitz and Blokesch, 2013; Seitz and Blokesch, 2014; Seitz et al., 2014; Ellison et al., 2018; Adams et al., 2019), environmental DNA is often heavily degraded and therefore short in size (Nielsen et al., 2007; Overballe-Petersen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Free DNA is thought to originate from dead and therefore less fit bacteria.
claims.source: In addition, free DNA is thought to originate from dead and therefore less fit bacteria, which renders the coding part of such genetic material non-favorable for naturally competent bacteria (Redfield, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Redfield, 1988.

claims.claim: V. cholerae actively acquires 'fresh' DNA from healthy, living bacteria through kin-discriminatory neighbor predation.
claims.source: In line with these arguments, we recently showed that V. cholerae does not solely rely on randomly released environmental DNA. Instead, it actively acquires 'fresh' DNA from healthy, living bacteria through kin-discriminatory neighbor predation (Borgeaud et al., 2015), which, conceptually, also occurs in other naturally competent bacteria (Veening and Blokesch, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research by the authors and others.

claims.claim: Neighbor predation in V. cholerae is accomplished by a contractile injection system known as the type VI secretion system (T6SS) that transports toxic effector proteins into prey.
claims.source: Neighbor predation in V. cholerae is accomplished by a contractile injection system known as the type VI secretion system (T6SS) that transports toxic effector proteins into prey (Ho et al., 2014; Cianfanelli et al., 2016; Galán and Waksman, 2018; Taylor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The T6SS of pandemic V. cholerae is co-regulated with its DNA-uptake machinery in a TfoX-, HapR-, and QstR-dependent manner when the bacterium grows on chitin.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the T6SS of pandemic V. cholerae is exquisitely co-regulated with its DNA-uptake machinery in a TfoX-, HapR-, and QstR-dependent manner when the bacterium grows on chitin (Borgeaud et al., 2015; Watve et al., 2015; Metzger et al., 2016; Jaskólska et al., 2018), which increases the chances of the competent bacterium to take up freshly released DNA compared to free-floating 'unfit' DNA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The coupling of competence and type VI secretion is conserved in several non-cholera vibrios.
claims.source: Notably, this coupling of competence and type VI secretion is also conserved in several non-cholera vibrios (Metzger et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The WT predator strain efficiently absorbed and integrated the prey-released resistance cassettes (aph or cat).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1, the WT predator strain efficiently absorbed and integrated the prey-released resistance cassettes (aph or cat), while the transformation efficiency for the T6SS-defective acceptor strain was significantly reduced (by 97.8% and 99.2% for aph and cat, respectively) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The transformation efficiency for the T6SS-defective acceptor strain was significantly reduced by 97.8% and 99.2% for aph and cat, respectively.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1, the WT predator strain efficiently absorbed and integrated the prey-released resistance cassettes (aph or cat), while the transformation efficiency for the T6SS-defective acceptor strain was significantly reduced (by 97.8% and 99.2% for aph and cat, respectively) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Comparable frequencies were observed for both selective markers (aph and cat), suggesting that their acquisition does not significantly affect the strains' fitness under non-selective conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, comparable frequencies were observed for both selective markers, suggesting that their acquisition does not significantly affect the strains' fitness under non-selective conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing similar transformation frequencies.

claims.claim: The comEA-minus strain was never transformed under predator-prey co-culture conditions, confirming that the gene transfer depended entirely on natural competence.
claims.source: We tested whether these transfer events were indeed competence-mediated and not based on other modes of HGT using a strain with a competence-related DNA import deficiency in that it lacked the competence protein ComEA that reels external DNA into the periplasm (Seitz et al., 2014). This comEA-minus strain was never transformed under these predator-prey co-culture conditions, confirming that the gene transfer did depend entirely on natural competence.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding that confirms the mechanism of gene transfer.

claims.claim: Double-resistance acquisition occurred at lower rates compared to single-resistant clones and were mostly below the limit of detection for the T6SS-minus acceptor strain.
claims.source: Next, we scored the frequencies of transformants that had adopted resistance against both antibiotics, which would show the possibility of two transformation events or the transfer of a large piece of DNA (indicated by the distance between the two genes on the same chromosome). These transformations occurred, as expected, at lower rates compared to single-resistant clones and were mostly below the limit of detection for the T6SS-minus acceptor strain (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A gradual decrease in the frequencies was observed the further the two resistance genes were apart from each other on the same chromosome.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed a gradual decrease in the frequencies the further the two resistance genes were apart from each other on the same chromosome, while a sharp drop occurred in the number of recovered transformants when the two resistance genes were carried on the two separate prey chromosomes (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A sharp drop occurred in the number of recovered transformants when the two resistance genes were carried on the two separate prey chromosomes.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed a gradual decrease in the frequencies the further the two resistance genes were apart from each other on the same chromosome, while a sharp drop occurred in the number of recovered transformants when the two resistance genes were carried on the two separate prey chromosomes (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: When the two resistance genes are carried in trans, at least two separate DNA-uptake events are required.
claims.source: While the latter scenario unambiguously requires at least two separate DNA-uptake events, the former, in which the resistance markers are carried in cis, could reflect a mix between single and multiple DNA absorption and integration events.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the mechanism of DNA uptake.

claims.claim: When purified genomic DNA was provided, the in cis double-resistance acquisition efficiencies reached a comparable range to the in trans efficiencies when the two resistance genes were separated by at least 100 kbp.
claims.source: When purified genomic DNA was instead provided as the transforming material to simplify the experiment and provide measurable results for all conditions, the in cis double-resistance acquisition efficiencies reached a comparable range to the in trans efficiencies when the two resistance genes were separated by at least 100 kbp.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the purified DNA experiments.

claims.claim: Transformations of less than 100 kbp likely often occurred through a single acquisition.
claims.source: This suggested that the more efficient transformations of less than 100 kbp likely often occurred through a single acquisition (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The WT predator and T6SS-minus acceptor behaved similarly when purified DNA was provided.
claims.source: Furthermore, the WT predator and T6SS-minus acceptor behaved similarly when purified DNA was provided, which makes sense as the need for active DNA release through neighbor predation was eliminated.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with an inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Neighbor predation might foster the transfer of long DNA stretches, which frequently exceeded 50 kbp.
claims.source: Based on these data and the fact that the double-acquisition rates for the T6SS-minus acceptor strain were mostly below the detection limit in the prey scenario (Figure 1B), we hypothesized that neighbor predation might foster the transfer of long DNA stretches, which frequently exceeded 50 kbp and therefore carry significant coding capacity.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Long DNA stretches released from killed prey might saturate the system against uptake of additional fragments.
claims.source: Moreover, the significantly lower double-acquisition rates when both cassettes are located in trans (e.g., on two different chromosomes) for the co-culturing conditions compared to the supplementation of purified gDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) led us speculate that long DNA stretches might be released from the killed prey thereby saturating the system against uptake of additional fragments.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: A1552 is a pandemic O1 El Tor strain belonging to the LAT-1 sublineage of the West-African South American (WASA) lineage of seventh pandemic V. cholerae strains.
claims.source: A1552 is a pandemic O1 El Tor strain (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1998) belonging to the LAT-1 sublineage of the West-African South American (WASA) lineage of seventh pandemic V. cholerae strains (Domman et al., 2017) while strain Sa5Y was isolated from the Californian Coast (Keymer et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Strain Sa5Y was isolated from the Californian Coast.
claims.source: A1552 is a pandemic O1 El Tor strain (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1998) belonging to the LAT-1 sublineage of the West-African South American (WASA) lineage of seventh pandemic V. cholerae strains (Domman et al., 2017) while strain Sa5Y was isolated from the Californian Coast (Keymer et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The environmental isolate Sa5Y lacked several genomic regions including VPI-1, VPI-2, VSP-I, VSP-II, the cholera toxin prophage CTX, and the WASA-1 element.
claims.source: Indeed, as expected from its non-clinical origin, the environmental isolate lacked several genomic regions, including those that encode major virulence features, namely Vibrio pathogenicity islands 1 and 2 (VPI-1, VPI-2), Vibrio seventh pandemic islands I and II (VSP-I, VSP-II; Dziejman et al., 2005), the cholera toxin prophage CTX (Waldor and Mekalanos, 1996), and the WASA-1 element.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomics analysis presented in the study.

claims.claim: The O-antigen cluster of Sa5Y differed significantly from the O1-encoding genes of pandemic strain A1552.
claims.source: In addition, the strain's O-antigen cluster differed significantly from the O1-encoding genes of pandemic strain A1552 (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomics analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The integron island differed the most between strains A1552 and Sa5Y.
claims.source: The region that differed the most between both strains was the integron island, which is consistent with the role of this assembly platform in fostering the incorporation of exogenous open reading frames (Mazel, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomics analysis with a citation supporting the interpretation.

claims.claim: The overall SNP frequency between A1552 and Sa5Y is approximately 1 in 55 nucleotides for conserved genes.
claims.source: Given these major differences between strain A1552 and Sa5Y and, in addition, an overall SNP frequency of approximately 1 in 55 nucleotides for conserved genes, we concluded that HGT events occurring between these two strains on chitinous surfaces could be precisely scored using short-read sequencing.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomics analysis.

claims.claim: The pandemic strains and Sa5Y contained nine or ten rRNA clusters in total compared to the initially reported eight.
claims.source: Apart from this important genomic information, we also noted that the pandemic strains as well as Sa5Y contained previously unrecognized rRNA operons, with nine or ten rRNA clusters in total compared to the initially reported eight (Heidelberg et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the genomic analysis that corrects previous reports.

claims.claim: Kanamycin-resistant transformants of A1552 were selected at an average frequency of 1.8 × 10−4 after 30 hr co-culturing on chitin.
claims.source: Using this system, resistant transformants of A1552 were selected at an average frequency of 1.8 × 10−4 after the 30 hr co-culturing on chitin, and 20 of those transformants were randomly picked for further analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the co-culture experiments.

claims.claim: The location and the size of the prey-donated genomic region differed significantly between most transformants.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3, apart from the common acquisition of the aph resistance cassette, the location and the size of the prey-donated genomic region differed significantly between most transformants.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The average length of total acquired DNA was previously estimated to be ~23 kbp in experiments using purified donor gDNA.
claims.source: Previous estimates of the average length of total acquired DNA were made in experiments using purified donor gDNA and were considered to be ~23 kbp (Miller et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The average length of the total acquired DNA in the current experiments was almost 70 kbp.
claims.source: Importantly, we observed in these new experiments that the average length of the total acquired DNA, meaning the DNA surrounding the aph cassette plus any transferred regions elsewhere on either of the two chromosomes, was almost 70 kbp and therefore significantly larger than the previous estimates.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: Around 15% of all transformants acquired and integrated more than 100 kbp.
claims.source: Around 15% of all transformants acquired and integrated more than 100 kbp (Figure 3B), which was previously considered unlikely due to rareness of such long DNA fragments in the environment.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The new DNA was acquired through double homologous recombination such that it replaced the initial DNA region and the overall genome size did not significantly change.
claims.source: Consistent with the principle of natural transformation, it should be noted that the new DNA was acquired through double homologous recombination such that it replaced the initial DNA region and the overall genome size did not significantly change.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data consistent with the known mechanism of natural transformation.

claims.claim: About 50% of the strains experienced a single HGT event around the aph cassette, while the others exchanged regions in up to eight different locations on the two chromosomes.
claims.source: Further analysis indicated that about 50% of the strains experienced a single HGT event around the aph cassette, while the others exchanged regions in up to eight different locations on the two chromosomes (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The length of continuous DNA stretches acquired from the prey ranged from a few kbp up to 168 kbp.
claims.source: Finally, we analyzed the length of continuous DNA stretches that were acquired from the prey and observed that those ranged from a few kbp up to 168 kbp (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: V. cholerae can acquire large genomic regions from killed neighbors with an average exchange of more than 50 kbp or ~50 genes.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that V. cholerae can acquire large genomic regions from killed neighbors with an average exchange of more than 50 kbp or ~50 genes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The observed recombination events were significantly larger than the mean recombination event size of ~4 kbp recently reported for surface-grown Streptococcus pneumoniae.
claims.source: Notably, our observed recombination events were significantly larger than the mean recombination event size of ~4 kbp that was recently reported for surface-grown Streptococcus pneumoniae (Cowley et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previous research supported by citation.

claims.claim: The findings contradict the notion that natural transformation is unlikely to serve DNA repair purposes or for the acquisition of new genetic information due to the quick fragmentation of free DNA in natural environments.
claims.source: Their data combined with our findings therefore contradict the notion that natural transformation is unlikely to serve DNA repair purposes or for the acquisition of new genetic information due to the quick fragmentation of free DNA in natural environments (Nielsen et al., 2007; Overballe-Petersen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in comparison to previous literature.

claims.claim: When gDNA was added at the start of the chitin-dependent culture, no transformants were reproducibly detected from three independent biological experiments.
claims.source: Notably, when the gDNA was added at the start of the chitin-dependent culture, no transformants were reproducibly detected from three independent biological experiments, suggesting that free DNA is rapidly degraded under such conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claims.claim: Free DNA is rapidly degraded when added at the start of chitin-dependent culture.
claims.source: Notably, when the gDNA was added at the start of the chitin-dependent culture, no transformants were reproducibly detected from three independent biological experiments, suggesting that free DNA is rapidly degraded under such conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of no transformants.

claims.claim: V. cholerae produces an extracellular and periplasmic nuclease Dns that degrades transforming material.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with our previous work in which we demonstrated that V. cholerae produces an extracellular and periplasmic nuclease Dns (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008; Seitz and Blokesch, 2014) that degrades transforming material.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claims.claim: At high cell density, dns is partially repressed through direct binding of HapR.
claims.source: At high cell density (HCD), where competence is induced, dns is partially repressed through direct binding of HapR (Blokesch and Schoolnik, 2008; Lo Scrudato and Blokesch, 2013), and this repression is reinforced by the transcription factor QstR (Lo Scrudato and Blokesch, 2013; Jaskólska et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The simultaneous expression of both machineries (T6SS and DNA uptake), concomitantly with a strong repression of dns, is a prerequisite for successful DNA transfer.
claims.source: We therefore concluded that the simultaneous expression of both machineries, concomitantly with a strong repression of dns, is a prerequisite for successful DNA transfer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Coordinated expression of T6SS and DNA uptake ensures that T6SS-mediated attacks are exquisitely timed with low nuclease activity so that the prey-released DNA can be efficiently absorbed.
claims.source: Indeed, such coordinated expression would ensure that T6SS-mediated attacks are exquisitely timed with low nuclease activity so that the prey-released DNA can be efficiently absorbed.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Adding purified gDNA after ~20–24 hr of growth on chitin led to similar transformation frequencies as those observed for the prey-released DNA caused by T6SS attacks.
claims.source: As we previously showed that the addition of purified gDNA after ~20–24 hr of growth on chitin wasn't prone to degradation by Dns (Marvig and Blokesch, 2010), we next choose this time point to probe the DNA acquisition capability using purified DNA (condition ②; Figure 4A). Doing so led to similar transformation frequencies as those observed for the prey-released DNA caused by T6SS attacks (condition ①; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: WGS of transformants from condition ② resulted in similar DNA acquisition patterns with average and maximum DNA acquisitions of 70 kbp and 188 kbp, respectively.
claims.source: WGS of 20 transformants from two biologically independent experiments likewise resulted in similar DNA acquisition patterns with average and maximum DNA acquisitions of 70 kbp and 188 kbp, respectively, and the presence of multiple exchanged regions of varying sizes (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The maximum DNA acquisition length of single fragments is probably reached between 100–110 kbp.
claims.source: While we cannot entirely exclude that the maximum length of individual DNA stretches was biased by the purification step, despite the fact that we chose a method that was designed for chromosomal DNA isolation of 20–150 kbp sized fragments (see Materials and methods), our results suggest that the maximum DNA acquisition length of single fragments is probably reached between 100–110 kbp (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data with acknowledgment of potential technical limitations.

claims.claim: The comparable acquisition patterns between conditions ① and ② imply that the prey-released DNA in condition ① is neither heavily fragmented nor is its accessibility or absorption significantly hindered.
claims.source: Moreover, the comparable acquisition patterns between conditions ① and ② (Figure 4) imply that the prey-released DNA in condition ① is neither heavily fragmented nor is its accessibility or absorption by the competent acceptor bacterium significantly hindered due to, for example, DNA-binding proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of experimental conditions.

claims.claim: Similar transformation frequencies were observed independent of the position of the aph cassette.
claims.source: Since the aph cassette was located within the T6SS sheath protein gene vipA in the above experiments, we wondered if this T6SS inactivation biased the DNA transfer efficiency. We therefore repeated the above-described experiments using prey strains that carried the aph cassette on the opposite site of chr 2 (within gene VCA0747; condition ③). As shown in (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), similar transformation frequencies were observed independent of the position of the aph cassette.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: WGS of transformants from condition ③ showed similar average and maximum DNA acquisition values (55.7 kbp and 227.4 kbp, respectively).
claims.source: Moreover, WGS of 2 × 20 transformants showed similar average and maximum DNA acquisition values (55.7 kbp and 227.4 kbp, respectively; Figure 4) as well as similar distribution patterns around the resistance marker (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Transformants with only single/connected exchanges dropped from ~50% in condition ① to around 20% in condition ③.
claims.source: However, while not statistically supported, it appeared as if these conditions were prone to the acquisition of multiple non-connected regions, as transformants with only single/connected exchanges dropped from ~50% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for condition ①) to around 20% (Figure 4—figure supplement 4 for condition ③).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data, though not statistically significant.

claims.claim: The restored T6SS-mediated killing capacity of the prey may lead to additional release of genomic DNA from the predator, which interferes with the uptake of prey-released DNA.
claims.source: Based on this observation, we hypothesized that the now-restored T6SS-mediated killing capacity of the prey led to the additional release of genomic DNA from the predator, which interfered with the uptake of prey-released DNA.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: No statistically significant differences were observed between conditions ③ and ④ for all tested characteristics including transformation frequency, number of exchanges, and separate and collective length.
claims.source: No statistically significant differences were observed between both conditions (③ and ④) for all tested characteristics including transformation frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), number of exchanges, and separate and collective length (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5), suggesting that predator-released DNA does not interfere with the predator's overall transformability by the prey-released DNA.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Predator-released DNA does not interfere with the predator's overall transformability by the prey-released DNA.
claims.source: No statistically significant differences were observed between both conditions (③ and ④) for all tested characteristics including transformation frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), number of exchanges, and separate and collective length (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5), suggesting that predator-released DNA does not interfere with the predator's overall transformability by the prey-released DNA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of statistical differences between conditions.

claims.claim: When both donor and acceptor strains were T6SS-defective, the transformation frequency dropped by 99.7%.
claims.source: We next tested whether T6SS-mediated DNA release impacted the length of the exchanged region, which would support the above speculation that the intimate co-regulation of type VI secretion, nuclease repression, and DNA uptake ensures that freshly released DNA is rapidly absorbed by the predator and is therefore less prone to fragmentation. Such co-regulation would not hold true for T6SS-independent DNA release as a result of random cell lysis, so we tested the transfer efficiency of the aph cassette under conditions in which both donor and acceptor strains were T6SS-defective (condition ⑤; Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 6). Under such conditions, the transformation frequency dropped by 99.7% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and WGS of 2 × 20 of these rare transformants showed significant differences.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The average and maximal length of acquired DNA and the number of exchanged regions were significantly different when T6SS+ versus T6SS- acceptor strains were compared.
claims.source: Indeed, the average and maximal length of acquired DNA (Figure 4B) and the number of exchanged regions (Figure 4C) were significantly different when T6SS+ versus T6SS- acceptor strains were compared, with the latter exchanges never exceeding four events compared to up to 13 events for T6SS-mediated DNA release (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: T6SS-mediated DNA acquisition increases the transfer efficiency by ~100 fold and fosters the exchange of multiple DNA stretches of extended lengths.
claims.source: Based on these data, we conclude that T6SS-mediated DNA acquisition not only increases the transfer efficiency by ~100 fold but also fosters the exchange of multiple DNA stretches of extended lengths.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing T6SS+ and T6SS- conditions.

claims.claim: Comparing conditions ⑥ (co-culture conditions) and ⑧ (prey-derived purified gDNA) revealed a small but significant transformation increase for the latter condition (~4 fold).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, the aph cassette was again transferred with high efficiency from the killed prey strain to the acceptor strain. However, comparing conditions ⑥ (co-culture conditions) and ⑧ (prey-derived purified gDNA as transforming material) revealed a small but significant transformation increase for the latter condition (~4 fold; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The larger size of chr 1 (~3 Mb) compared to chr 2 (~1 Mb) slightly lowers the probability of acquiring the aph cassette when released from the killed prey that carried the resistance marker on chr 1.
claims.source: Based on these data, we speculate that the larger size of chr 1 (~3 Mb) compared to chr 2 (~1 Mb) slightly lowers the probability of acquiring the aph cassette when released from the killed prey that carried the resistance marker on chr 1.

claims.source: Consistent with this idea was the finding that purified gDNA from all those prey strains described in this study resulted in the same level of transformation no matter where the selective marker was located (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: The average and maximum DNA acquisition values for transformants with markers on chromosome 1 were highly comparable to those for DNA exchanges on chromosome 2.
claims.source: Next, we randomly picked 20 transformants from two biologically independent experiments for each of these three experimental conditions (⑥ to ⑧) and sequenced their genomes (Figure 4—figure supplements 7 to 9). The analysis of these transformants showed that the average and maximum DNA acquisition values were highly comparable to those described above for DNA exchanges on chromosome 2 (Figure 4B) and that multiple exchanged regions were likewise observed (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Prey-derived transforming DNA can equally modify both chromosomes.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that prey-derived transforming DNA can equally modify both chromosomes.

claims.source: Moreover, our data suggest that consecutive stretches of exchanged DNA above ~200 kbp either do not occur or occur at levels below the detection limit of this study, and that this size limitation is not caused by the toxin/antitoxin–module-containing integron island on chr 2.

claims.source: Based on the data presented above, we conclude that T6SS-mediated predation followed by DNA uptake leads to the exchange of large DNA regions that can bring about bacterial evolution.

claims.claim: Heterogeneous environmental V. cholerae populations were observed in cholera-endemic areas.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with the heterogeneous environmental V. cholerae populations that were observed in cholera-endemic areas (Faruque et al., 2004).

claims.claim: The work shows the incredible DNA exchange potential that chitin-induced V. cholerae strains exert under co-culture conditions.
claims.source: Notably, our work shows the incredible DNA exchange potential that chitin-induced V. cholerae strains exert under co-culture conditions and future studies are therefore required to better understand strain diversity in clinical and environmental settings in the absence of sampling biases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

results.result: The T6SS significantly enhances DNA transformation efficiency in V. cholerae. WT predator strains efficiently absorbed prey-released resistance cassettes, while T6SS-defective acceptor strains showed 97.8-99.2% reduction in transformation efficiency. The comEA-minus strain was never transformed, confirming the process depends entirely on natural competence.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 provide quantitative experimental data showing dramatic reduction in transformation when T6SS is absent, and C30 provides a critical negative control confirming the mechanism. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls.

results.result: Double-resistance acquisition patterns suggest that V. cholerae can transfer DNA fragments exceeding 100 kbp in single events. Transformation frequencies decreased with increasing distance between markers on the same chromosome, with a sharp drop when markers were on separate chromosomes. With purified DNA, in cis double-resistance acquisition reached comparable levels to in trans when markers were ≥100 kbp apart, suggesting single acquisitions often occur for fragments <100 kbp.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 present a logical progression of experimental observations with appropriate controls (purified DNA vs. co-culture). The distance-dependent pattern and the distinction between cis and trans configurations provide strong evidence for the size of transferred DNA fragments. The inference in C36 is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Comparative genomics revealed substantial differences between pandemic strain A1552 and environmental isolate Sa5Y. Sa5Y lacked major virulence regions (VPI-1, VPI-2, VSP-I, VSP-II, CTX, WASA-1), had a different O-antigen cluster, and showed ~1 SNP per 55 nucleotides in conserved genes. Both strains contained 9-10 rRNA clusters, correcting previous reports of 8 clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 describe genomic characterization supported by long-read PacBio sequencing and comparative analysis. The findings are consistent with expected differences between pandemic and environmental strains. The correction of rRNA cluster numbers (C46) is a valuable observation, though the authors acknowledge potential assembly artifacts in previous work.

results.result: Whole-genome sequencing of transformants revealed that V. cholerae acquires large genomic regions from killed neighbors, with an average of ~70 kbp (significantly larger than previous estimates of ~23 kbp). Approximately 15% of transformants acquired >100 kbp, 50% experienced single HGT events, while others exchanged regions at up to 8 locations. Individual DNA stretches ranged from a few kbp to 168 kbp.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C55 present the core WGS findings with clear quantitative data from 60 transformants across 3 biological replicates. The results substantially revise previous estimates and are supported by detailed genomic analysis. The conclusion in C55 is well-justified by the data.

results.result: The observed recombination events in V. cholerae (~70 kbp average) are significantly larger than those reported for S. pneumoniae (~4 kbp), contradicting the notion that natural transformation is unlikely to serve DNA repair or acquisition purposes due to rapid DNA fragmentation in natural environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C56 and C58 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing literature. The comparison to S. pneumoniae is valid and the conclusion challenges previous assumptions about environmental DNA degradation. The inference is well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: Timing of DNA availability is critical for transformation success. When gDNA was added at the start of chitin-dependent culture, no transformants were detected, suggesting rapid DNA degradation. This is consistent with V. cholerae producing the nuclease Dns, which is repressed at high cell density when competence is induced. Coordinated expression of T6SS, DNA uptake machinery, and dns repression is required for successful DNA transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 present a mechanistic explanation supported by experimental observations (C59) and previous work on Dns (C61-C62). The conclusion about coordinated expression (C63-C64) is a reasonable inference from the data, though C64 is somewhat speculative about the precise timing mechanism.

results.result: Adding purified gDNA after 20-24 hr of chitin growth (when dns is repressed) resulted in similar transformation frequencies and DNA acquisition patterns as T6SS-mediated prey killing, with average and maximum acquisitions of 70 kbp and 188 kbp respectively. The maximum single-fragment acquisition length is likely 100-110 kbp. The comparable patterns suggest prey-released DNA is neither heavily fragmented nor significantly hindered in accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide important comparative data between conditions ① and ②. The inference in C67 appropriately acknowledges potential technical limitations from the purification method. The conclusion in C68 is well-supported by the similarity between conditions, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: The position of the resistance cassette (vipA vs. VCA0747) did not significantly affect transformation frequency or overall DNA acquisition patterns. However, transformants with single/connected exchanges appeared to decrease from ~50% to ~20% when prey T6SS was functional, though this was not statistically significant. No significant differences were observed when prey T6SS was inactivated by a non-selected marker, suggesting predator-released DNA does not interfere with transformation by prey-released DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 show consistent results, but C71 explicitly notes the observation is not statistically supported. The hypothesis in C72 is speculative, and while C73-C74 provide negative results that refute this hypothesis, the authors acknowledge technical limitations (inability to detect complete revertants). The overall conclusion requires more rigorous statistical support.

results.result: T6SS-mediated DNA acquisition dramatically enhances transformation efficiency and DNA transfer size. When both donor and acceptor were T6SS-defective, transformation frequency dropped 99.7%, and the average/maximal DNA length and number of exchanges were significantly reduced (maximum 4 events vs. up to 13 for T6SS-mediated release). T6SS-mediated acquisition increases transfer efficiency ~100-fold and fosters exchange of multiple extended DNA stretches.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 provide strong quantitative evidence for the role of T6SS in DNA transfer. The comparison between T6SS+ and T6SS- conditions is well-controlled and statistically significant. The ~100-fold enhancement and the differences in DNA acquisition patterns provide compelling support for the conclusion.

results.result: DNA transfer occurs efficiently on both chromosomes. When the resistance marker was on chromosome 1, there was a small (~4-fold) but significant reduction in transformation frequency compared to purified DNA, possibly due to the larger size of chr 1 (~3 Mb) vs. chr 2 (~1 Mb) reducing the relative probability of cassette acquisition. However, purified gDNA from all prey strains showed equal transformation regardless of marker location, and WGS analysis showed comparable DNA acquisition patterns for both chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 address whether chromosome size affects transformation. The speculation in C79-C80 is reasonable given the size difference, and C81 provides supporting evidence. The WGS data in C82 and conclusion in C83 are well-supported, though the ~4-fold difference is modest and alternative explanations are not fully explored.

results.result: Consecutive DNA stretches above ~200 kbp either do not occur or occur below the detection limit, and this size limitation is not caused by the toxin/antitoxin-module-containing integron island on chromosome 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 present a negative result that is important for understanding the limits of DNA transfer. The conclusion is supported by the absence of such events across all conditions tested, including those involving chromosome 1 (which lacks the integron island). However, the authors appropriately acknowledge the detection limit caveat.

results.result: T6SS-mediated predation followed by DNA uptake leads to exchange of large DNA regions that can accelerate bacterial evolution. This is consistent with heterogeneous V. cholerae populations in endemic areas and demonstrates the incredible DNA exchange potential of chitin-induced V. cholerae under co-culture conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 and C95 present the main conclusions of the study. The inference about evolutionary impact is well-supported by the extensive experimental data showing large-scale DNA transfer. The consistency with field observations (C87) strengthens the ecological relevance, though direct evidence of evolutionary acceleration would require additional experiments.

results.result: Despite the demonstrated DNA exchange potential, pandemic cholera isolates appear clonal. Two explanations are proposed: sampling bias toward pathogenic strains, and spread of transformation-inhibiting nucleases in pandemic strains. IVIAT data showing immune responses to competence pilus proteins suggest bacteria encounter competence-inducing conditions before or during infection, though in vivo expression data from volunteers does not support post-colonization competence induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 address an apparent paradox. C88 is well-supported by citations, but C89 is explicitly speculative. C90 has some experimental support but is limited to specific mobile elements. The IVIAT data (C91-C92) are interesting but the inference in C93 is uncertain, and C94 contradicts one possibility. This section raises important questions but does not definitively resolve the paradox.

results.result: Natural competence for transformation is a primary mode of horizontal gene transfer in which bacteria absorb free DNA and integrate it via homologous recombination. V. cholerae uses its T6SS to actively acquire DNA from non-kin neighbors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C8-C10 describe established knowledge about natural competence, supported by appropriate citations. C3 references the authors' previous work on T6SS-mediated DNA acquisition. These provide essential background context and are well-supported by the literature.

results.result: Competence induction in V. cholerae is tightly regulated by chitin sensing and quorum sensing. Growth on chitin induces TfoX production, which activates DNA-uptake machinery. HapR represses the nuclease dns and co-activates QstR with TfoX, which further represses dns and activates DNA-uptake genes. The T6SS is co-regulated with DNA-uptake machinery in a TfoX-, HapR-, and QstR-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 and C25 describe the regulatory network controlling competence, all supported by multiple citations to previous work. This provides important mechanistic context for understanding the experimental results. The co-regulation of T6SS and competence (C25) is particularly relevant to the study's findings.

results.result: Environmental DNA is typically degraded and originates from dead bacteria, making it less favorable for competent bacteria. V. cholerae overcomes this by actively acquiring DNA from living bacteria through T6SS-mediated neighbor predation. This coupling of competence and T6SS is conserved in several vibrios.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 and C26 establish the rationale for the study by describing limitations of environmental DNA and the T6SS-based solution. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. This provides crucial context for why the study's findings are significant.

results.result: Comparable transformation frequencies for both selective markers suggest acquisition does not significantly affect fitness. The data led to the hypothesis that neighbor predation fosters transfer of long DNA stretches (>50 kbp), and that such stretches might saturate the uptake system against additional fragments.
results.evaluation: C29 presents a reasonable inference from similar frequencies, though fitness effects under selective pressure are not tested. C38 is explicitly a hypothesis based on preliminary data. C39 is speculation about mechanism. While these claims provide useful interpretive context, they require additional experimental validation.

results.result: V. cholerae has caused seven pandemics since 1817, affecting 1-4 million people annually. Previous work showed V. cholerae can exchange large genomic regions (e.g., ~40 kbp O139-antigen cluster), though the prevalence of sufficiently long non-degraded DNA in the environment has been questioned.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 provide epidemiological context supported by WHO data. C11 references previous work by the authors demonstrating large-scale genetic exchange. C12 establishes the scientific controversy that motivates the current study. All claims are appropriately supported by citations.
